q: What is the chemical symbol for gold?
fact: Gold is so malleable that a single gram can be beaten into a sheet covering about half a square metre.

q: Which gas do plants take in from the air to make their food?
fact: The oxygen plants release during photosynthesis comes from splitting water molecules, not from the carbon dioxide.

q: How many bones are there in an adult human body?
fact: Babies are born with around 300 bones, but many of them fuse together as they grow.

q: In which part of the body is the stapes, the smallest bone?
fact: The stapes is roughly the size of a grain of rice, and its name is Latin for 'stirrup', which it resembles.

q: At sea level, at what temperature in Celsius does water boil?
fact: At the top of Mount Everest the air pressure is so low that water boils at only around 70°C.

q: Which element has the chemical symbol K?
fact: The K comes from 'kalium', a word traced back to the Arabic for plant ashes, where potassium compounds were first found.

q: Which scientist developed the theory of general relativity?
fact: Satellite navigation has to correct for relativity, or GPS positions would drift by roughly 10 km every day.

q: What is the hardest natural substance on Earth?
fact: Diamond and graphite, the 'lead' in pencils, are both made of pure carbon, just with the atoms arranged differently.

q: Which organ in the human body produces insulin?
fact: The first person ever treated with insulin was 14-year-old Leonard Thompson, in Toronto in January 1922.

q: Which part of the brain is only about 10% of its volume but holds over half its neurons?
fact: The cerebellum helps coordinate balance and movement, and its name is Latin for 'little brain'.

q: Which temperature scale starts at absolute zero?
fact: William Thomson became a Glasgow professor at 22 and later took the title Lord Kelvin from the river beside the university.

q: Which gas makes up most of the Earth's atmosphere?
fact: Argon makes up almost 1% of the air, and its name comes from the Greek for 'lazy' because it barely reacts with anything.

q: Roughly how fast does light travel in a vacuum?
fact: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes and 20 seconds to travel from the Sun to the Earth.

q: Who discovered penicillin in 1928?
fact: Fleming spotted mould killing bacteria on a culture dish that had been left out while he was away on holiday.

q: Which element did Marie Curie name after her home country?
fact: Her laboratory notebooks are still radioactive and are kept in lead-lined boxes at France's national library in Paris.

q: Which element was detected in the Sun before it was found on Earth?
fact: It showed up as a mysterious yellow line in sunlight during an 1868 eclipse, but wasn't isolated on Earth until 1895.

q: What is the largest organ of the human body?
fact: As well as protecting you, your skin makes vitamin D when it is exposed to sunlight.

q: In DNA, which base always pairs with adenine?
fact: If you unravelled the DNA from just one of your cells and laid it end to end, it would stretch about 2 metres.

q: Which blood type is known as the universal donor for red blood cells?
fact: Austrian scientist Karl Landsteiner discovered the ABO blood groups in 1901 and later won a Nobel Prize for it.

q: Scurvy is caused by a lack of which vitamin?
fact: Royal Navy sailors were given lime juice to prevent scurvy, which is how British sailors got the nickname 'limeys'.

q: Which element has the atomic number 1?
fact: Hydrogen makes up roughly three-quarters of all the ordinary matter in the universe by mass.

q: What is the pH of pure water at 25°C?
fact: The pH scale was introduced in 1909 by Danish chemist Søren Sørensen while working at the Carlsberg brewery's laboratory.

q: Which metal is a liquid at room temperature?
fact: Another metal, gallium, melts at about 30°C, so a piece of it will turn liquid if you hold it in your hand.

q: How many chambers does the human heart have?
fact: An adult heart beats roughly 100,000 times a day, pumping blood around the whole body.

q: Which scientist wrote the Principia, setting out the laws of motion?
fact: Newton later ran the Royal Mint, where he personally investigated counterfeiters.

q: Lightning can heat the air to roughly five times hotter than what?
fact: Thunder is the sound of air expanding explosively after being heated by a lightning bolt in a fraction of a second.

q: The microwave oven was invented after what melted in an engineer's pocket?
fact: The first food Percy Spencer deliberately cooked with microwaves was popcorn.

q: At roughly what temperature does a popcorn kernel pop?
fact: The popping sound isn't the hull splitting: it comes from steam suddenly escaping from inside the kernel.

q: Which subatomic particle carries a negative electric charge?
fact: J.J. Thomson discovered the electron in 1897 at the Cavendish Laboratory in Cambridge.

q: Which part of the eye controls how much light gets in?
fact: The word 'iris' comes from the Greek for rainbow, a nod to the many different eye colours.

q: Who created the periodic table of elements in 1869?
fact: He left gaps for elements not yet discovered and correctly predicted the properties of gallium and germanium.

q: Which is the most abundant element in the Earth's crust?
fact: Taking the whole planet into account, iron is the most abundant element by mass, mostly locked away in the core.

q: Which vitamin is essential for helping blood to clot?
fact: Its letter comes from 'Koagulation', the German and Danish spelling, after its discovery by Danish scientist Henrik Dam.

q: Which metal is the best conductor of electricity?
fact: Copper is used for most wiring because it conducts almost as well but costs far less.

q: Which part of a cell is often called its 'powerhouse'?
fact: Mitochondria have their own DNA, which is almost always inherited from your mother.

q: Who coined the word 'cell' after looking at cork under a microscope?
fact: He chose the word because the tiny boxes reminded him of the small rooms, or cells, that monks lived in.

q: What is the chemical symbol for tungsten?
fact: The W comes from its other name, wolfram, and tungsten has the highest melting point of any metal, about 3,422°C.

q: Which is the strongest of the four fundamental forces of nature?
fact: Gravity is by far the weakest: a small fridge magnet can hold a paperclip up against the pull of the entire Earth.

q: Which scientist discovered electromagnetic induction in 1831?
fact: Faraday also started the Royal Institution's famous Christmas Lectures for young people, first held in 1825.

q: Which scientist discovered the neutron in 1932?
fact: Chadwick had worked under Ernest Rutherford, who had predicted the existence of the neutron back in 1920.
